![Eleven eco-hydrological basins and 70 catalogued Indigenous habitation complexes across mainland Australia and Tasmania from 10000BC to 1788.](figures/pre_1788_australia_regional_map.png)



# Abstract

Between the end of the Pleistocene in 10000BC and the arrival of the First Fleet at Port Jackson in 1788, the Indigenous population of mainland Australia and Tasmania expanded more than threefold across eleven organic eco-hydrological basins covering 7.895.042 km². Aggregate population rose from 223,2k (223.200) at 10000BC to 384,7k (384.700) in 5000BC, reached 600,2k (600.200) around year 0 and stood at 785k (785.000) on the eve of British colonisation in 1788, lifting mean continental density from 0,028 to 0,099 inhabitants per km² [@williams2013population; @bradshaw2021stochastic; @tobler2017aboriginal]. This long expansion was never uniform across the continent. Four well-watered riverine, temperate and monsoonal basins — the Murray-Darling Basin (185k, 23,6% of the 1788 total), the North-East Coast and Cape York (165k, 21%), the South-East Coast and Australian Alps (115k, 14,6%) and the Gulf of Carpentaria and Top End (108k, 13,8%) — covered 36,4% of Australia's surface yet supported 73% of its pre-contact people (573k), with coastal southeast densities climbing to 0,418 inhabitants per km². By contrast, the three arid interior zones — the Central Arid Western Plateau (21k, 0,011 per km²), the Lake Eyre Endorheic Basin (26k, 0,02 per km²) and the Nullarbor and Southern Gulfs (25k, 0,051 per km²) — encompassed 47,6% of continental area while holding just 9,2% of the population (72k). Separated from the mainland by post-glacial flooding of Bass Strait before 10000BC, Tasmania grew slowest of all eleven regions, moving from 3,2k to 6k (0,073 per km²) across nearly twelve millennia [@suman2016late]. Reconciling radiocarbon population curves, Pleistocene genomic phylogeography, epidemiological reassessment of early colonial smallpox and 70 catalogued Indigenous habitation complexes with 190 chronological observations, this study situates Australia's 1788 population firmly above early twentieth-century minimalist floors of 300k to 314,5k while remaining disciplined by ecological carrying capacity and Holocene climatic variance [@thornton1986our; @anon1984aboriginal; @hunter2015estimating].

# Background

## Sahul Colonisation and Pleistocene Demographic Foundations

Human occupation of Australia began long before the Holocene boundary of 10000BC, when lowered sea levels fused mainland Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into the single Pleistocene landmass of Sahul. Excavations at Madjedbebe in western Arnhem Land place initial human presence in northern Australia by 65.000 years ago, supported by optically stimulated luminescence chronologies and stone-tool assemblages containing ground-edge axes and ochre crayons [@clarkson2017human]. Recent archaeobotanical recovery from the same deep strata confirms that early colonists immediately exploited broad-spectrum plant foods, processing pandanus nuts, palms, roots and tubers across changing monsoonal regimes between 65.000 and 53.000 years ago [@florin2020first; @florin2021pandanus]. That archaeological long chronology aligns closely with recent mitogenomic and nuclear genomic reconstructions tracing dispersal out of Sunda across Wallacea into Sahul around 60.000 years ago via both a northern corridor into New Guinea and a southern maritime crossing through Timor into the Kimberley and Arnhem Land [@gandini2025genomic; @gomes2015human; @curnoe2016deep].

Crossing the Wallacean straits required deliberate, repeated open-water voyaging rather than accidental drift. Demographic drift-and-viability simulations indicate that permanent colonisation of Sahul demanded organised founder groups numbering at least 1.300 people arriving within a few centuries, equipped with seaworthy watercraft and intentional island-hopping logistics [@bird2019early]. Along the southern Timor threshold, stratified cave sequences show an abrupt intensification of human occupation by 44.000 years ago, while coastal Kimberley rockshelters confirm settled maritime economies along northwestern Australia by 50.000 years ago [@shipton2024abrupt; @norman2022human]. Once ashore on Sahul, mobile foraging groups dispersed rapidly across the continent's physiographic corridors. Least-cost pathway modelling and cellular-automaton simulations show that colonists tracked river systems, escarpment margins and prominent landscape landmarks as natural migration highways, occupying every major biome from tropical savanna to Tasmanian temperate valleys within roughly 5.000 to 10.000 years of landfall [@crabtree2021landscape; @bradshaw2021stochastic; @bradshaw2023directionall; @salles2024physiography].

Genomic evidence confirms how rapidly those pioneer communities settled into durable regional homelands. Whole-genome sequencing of Aboriginal Australians and Papuans indicates a deep population split around 37.000 years ago, followed by structured internal divergence across Australia beginning around 31.000 years ago [@malaspinas2016genomic]. Continental mitogenomic mapping further demonstrates that once coastal and interior bands established territories roughly 50.000 years ago, maternal lineages remained remarkably anchored to specific geographic regions for tens of millennia [@tobler2017aboriginal]. Cultural continuity matched that genetic stability: at Cloggs Cave in the foothills of the Australian Alps, hearth and ritual features tied directly to nineteenth-century Gunaikurnai ethnography date back 11.000 to 12.000 years to the close of the Last Ice Age [@david2024archaeologic].

Late Pleistocene demography was nevertheless shaped by severe climatic oscillation. Across eastern Sahul, palaeontological records at South Walker Creek and central Queensland point to prolonged environmental aridification and habitat contraction driving megafaunal extinction rather than abrupt continent-wide overkill, constraining both faunal ranges and human foraging options [@hocknull2020extinction; @gaete2025megafauna]. During the Last Glacial Maximum between roughly 22000BC and 16000BC, hyper-aridity and shifting dune fields forced desert bands to contract into well-watered cryptic refugia — the MacDonnell and Pilbara ranges, the Kimberley, Arnhem Land, coastal plains and the Murray-Darling riverine corridor — cutting continental population by an estimated 60% from earlier Pleistocene highs [@williams2013population; @mulvaney2020prehistory].

## Post-Glacial Sea-Level Rise and Holocene Intensification

As global temperatures rose after 16000BC, melting ice sheets inundated nearly two million km² of Sahul's continental shelf. Rising waters flooded the Arafura Plain between Australia and New Guinea around 6000BC and submerged the Bassian Plain between Victoria and Tasmania even earlier, severing Tasmania completely before 10000BC [@gandini2025genomic; @salles2024physiography]. Coastal communities retreated steadily inland across the Gulf of Carpentaria, the Kimberley shelf, the Great Australian Bight and Bass Strait, compressing coastal territories while creating productive new estuaries, barrier lagoons and mangrove swamps as sea levels stabilised near modern heights between 5000BC and 4000BC.

From 5000BC onward, Australian prehistory entered a decisive phase of regional demographic and economic expansion often termed Mid-to-Late Holocene intensification [@williams2015holocene; @florin2021pandanus]. Radiocarbon time-series across the continent register sustained population growth accompanied by technological diversification: the spread of backed artefacts and small-tool traditions, systematic grass-seed grinding in the arid and semi-arid interior, toxic-plant leaching of cycads and rainforest nuts in Queensland, and active landscape management through mosaic fire-stick farming and plant translocation — illustrated genetically by ancient human-mediated dispersal of the Australian baobab across northwestern Australia [@rangan2015genetic; @florin2020first]. Linguistically and genetically, Pama-Nyungan languages and associated gene flow spread across nearly seven-eighths of the mainland from a northeastern homeland during the Mid-Holocene without replacing deep regional maternal ancestry [@malaspinas2016genomic; @tobler2017aboriginal].

Between 2000BC and 1788, rising El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) amplitude introduced sharper drought cycles across eastern and central Australia, prompting flexible risk-buffering strategies rather than continental collapse [@williams2015holocene; @gaete2025megafauna]. In humid temperate, riverine and tropical belts, Indigenous nations engineered durable aquatic infrastructure and organised large periodic aggregations: stone eel channels, basalt weirs and stone-walled habitation clusters at Budj Bim and Toolondo in western Victoria; interlocking dry-stone fish traps along the Barwon River at Brewarrina; seasonal alpine Bogong moth harvests in the Snowy Mountains; triennial Bunya pine festivals drawing over 2.000 people to Booburrgan Ngmmunge in southern Queensland; and horticultural island villages across the Torres Strait [@mulvaney2020prehistory; @david2024archaeologic]. Along the Arnhem Land coast, regular seasonal visits by Makassan trepang fleets from Sulawesi after roughly 1700 introduced iron tools, dugout canoes and new exchange networks across coastal Yolŋu communities without displacing Indigenous political sovereignty [@wright2023archaeology].

## The Pre-1788 Demographic Debate

Estimating Australia's population in 1788 has been one of the sharpest quantitative controversies in historical demography. In 1930, the anthropologist A. R. Radcliffe-Brown compiled district-by-district colonial accounts and proposed a conservative continental minimum of roughly 250k to 300k inhabitants, a figure widely adopted for half a century [@mulvaney2020prehistory]. In 1980, L. R. Smith systematically audited colonial musters, protectorate returns and twentieth-century censuses to construct the historical series still reproduced in official Australian statistical tables, fixing a minimum contact baseline of 314.500 (314,5k) people — including just 15k in Victoria and 48k in New South Wales [@anon1984aboriginal].

That low consensus broke apart in 1983 when economic historian Noel Butlin published *Our Original Aggression*. By modelling the catastrophic mortality of the 1789 Port Jackson smallpox epidemic and a second wave sweeping the Murray-Darling basin in 1829 to 1831 — both of which raced ahead of European pastoralists — Butlin argued that colonial observers arrived in southeastern Australia only after virgin-soil epidemics had already cut Indigenous numbers by half or more [@thornton1986our]. Reversing those losses implied pre-contact populations in Victoria and New South Wales roughly three to five times larger than Radcliffe-Brown and Smith allowed, pushing continental totals past 750k and potentially above 1M [@thornton1986our; @mulvaney2020prehistory].

Subsequent scholarship tested Butlin's thesis from three independent angles. First, palaeodemographic reconstruction from more than 5.000 radiocarbon dates demonstrated steady Mid-to-Late Holocene expansion peaking around 1,2M during the last millennium before moderating slightly to roughly 750k to 1,2M by 1788 [@williams2013population; @williams2015holocene]. Second, genomic effective-population reconstructions and stochastic ecological models confirmed substantial Late Holocene carrying capacity across the eastern, northern and southwestern coastal rims [@bradshaw2021stochastic; @malaspinas2016genomic]. Third, Boyd Hunter and John Carmody re-examined the pathology of the 1789 and 1829 epidemics — weighing smallpox against chickenpox and pre-1788 Makassan viral pathways — and concluded that while specific epidemiological vectors remain debated, the archaeological and historical evidence firmly supports a 1788 continental population near 750k to 800k, far above Smith's 314,5k floor yet below extreme speculative ceilings of 3M [@hunter2015estimating].

# Methodology

## Organic Eco-Hydrological Regionalisation

Modern state borders cut arbitrarily across Indigenous drainage territories, ecological gradients and language networks. For the pre-colonial period from 10000BC to 1788, this chapter therefore partitions mainland Australia and Tasmania into eleven organic eco-hydrological basins aligned with major surface-water catchments, rainfall isohyets and Pleistocene-Holocene biogeographic barriers. Basin boundaries were digitised directly from HydroBASINS Level-6 drainage catchments and checked against physiographic and regional archaeological syntheses [@crabtree2021landscape; @salles2024physiography].

Each basin captures a coherent foraging and demographic regime. Four high-productivity regions anchor the humid rim and perennial rivers: the Murray-Darling Basin (1.086.964 km²), the North-East Coast and Cape York (598.813 km²), the South-East Coast and Australian Alps (275.121 km²) and the Gulf of Carpentaria and Top End (909.136 km²). Three transitional Mediterranean, monsoonal and semi-arid coastal belts form the western and northern flanks: South-West Australia covering Noongar country (318.147 km²), the Kimberley and Fitzroy Basin (309.369 km²) and the Pilbara and Western Coast (560.298 km²). Three interior and southern arid regions span the dry core: the Central Arid Western Plateau (1.969.743 km²), the Lake Eyre Endorheic Basin (1.299.106 km²) and the Nullarbor and Southern Gulfs (485.879 km²). Finally, Tasmania and the Bass Strait islands (82.465 km²) form a distinct insular basin isolated throughout the entire 10000BC to 1788 domain.

## Calibration of Benchmark Trajectories and Historical GIS Layers

Regional population totals are anchored at four primary chronological benchmarks — 10000BC, 5000BC, year 0 and 1788 — and linked to six Historical GIS (HGIS) polygon regimes spanning year 0, 500, 1000, 1500, 1700 and 1780 (66 polygon-year records across eleven HydroBASINS units totalling 7.726.164 km² of terrestrial catchment area, compared with 7.895.042 km² in the full coastal-inclusive areal mask). Rather than extrapolating linearly from a single colonial count, basin-level trajectories triangulate four converging lines of evidence:

First, regional summed probability distributions of archaeological radiocarbon dates track relative changes in human occupation intensity from the terminal Pleistocene through Mid-Holocene stabilisation and Late Holocene growth [@williams2013population; @williams2015holocene]. Second, ecological net primary productivity and freshwater availability bound maximum sustainable foraging densities across biomes, ranging from roughly 0,01 to 0,02 inhabitants per km² across hyper-arid dune fields up to 0,25 to 0,5 inhabitants per km² across perennial river estuaries, basalt wetlands and wet-tropical rainforests [@bradshaw2021stochastic; @bradshaw2023directionall]. Third, post-1788 colonial musters, protectorate estimates and epidemic back-projections anchor contact-era ratios between regions — particularly in northern and western regions reached later by pastoral settlement, where direct nineteenth-century enumeration suffered less prior depopulation [@anon1984aboriginal; @hunter2015estimating]. Fourth, ethnographic land-tenure and language-group density reconstructions corroborate higher contact densities along the Murray River, southwestern Victoria, Sydney Harbour, Moreton Bay, the Wet Tropics and Arnhem Land [@mulvaney2020prehistory; @burke2013archaeology].

Between benchmarks after year 0, sub-regional growth follows smooth compound rates calibrated to Late Holocene radiocarbon moderation, carrying the continental aggregate from 600,2k at year 0 through 646,9k in 500, 697,3k in 1000, 751,7k in 1500 and 774,7k in 1700 to 784,1k in 1780 and 785k in 1788. Spatial population rasters distribute each basin's total continuously according to river proximity, coastal productivity and palaeoclimatic suitability, avoiding artificial administrative steps along catchment divides.

## Evidence-Based Settlement Gazetteer Protocol

Because pre-1788 Australia contained no walled cities or state tax rolls, the companion settlement gazetteer catalogues 70 archaeologically and ethnohistorically documented habitation complexes, seasonal aggregation centres, aquaculture hubs, rockshelters and island villages carrying 190 dated population observations across the 10000BC to 1788 span. Candidates were audited through four sequential waves recorded in the chapter source ledger: Wave 1 assembled 64 primary entries from national heritage registers, archaeological site syntheses and colonial ethnohistorical baselines; Wave 2 added five peer-reviewed monograph complexes; Wave 3 reconciled longitudinal naming variants and consolidated six overlapping duplicate aliases within 25 km (Roonka, Laura Shelters, Lake Mungo, Puntutjarpa, Kow Swamp and Koonalda); and Wave 4 executed a sub-regional coverage sweep adding one final station (marginal gain 1,45%), achieving zero empty eco-hydrological basins and 0% crowd-sourced fallback share. Estimated populations represent peak local or seasonal aggregation headcounts grounded in primary archaeological and ethnohistorical monographs rather than modern census towns.

# Testing and Validation

## Cross-Checks Against Palaeodemographic and Epidemiological Benchmarks

To ensure that continental totals and regional densities sit securely within scholarly bounds, the 10000BC to 1788 series was tested against four independent baselines. At the terminal Pleistocene opening (10000BC), our continental figure of 223,2k (0,028 inhabitants per km²) reflects recovery from the Last Glacial Maximum trough while remaining substantially below Mid-to-Late Holocene levels. Williams's radiocarbon time-series models a Last Glacial Maximum low followed by steady Early Holocene rebound, placing Australia in the low hundreds of thousands by 10000BC before accelerating sharply after 5000BC [@williams2013population]. Similarly, stochastic Sahul simulations yield equilibrium Pleistocene densities of roughly 0,02 to 0,05 inhabitants per km² across productive margins and near-zero across hyper-arid basins, closely matching our 10000BC range from 0,003 per km² on the Central Arid Western Plateau to 0,116 along the South-East Coast [@bradshaw2021stochastic; @bradshaw2023directionall].

At the 1788 contact horizon, our continental total of 785k (0,099 inhabitants per km²) reconciles the long-running dispute between colonial minimalists and epidemiological revisionists. It stands 2,5 times higher than L. R. Smith's conservative 1980 minimum of 314,5k — reflecting the consensus established after Butlin that southeastern Australia suffered severe virgin-soil smallpox losses prior to systematic British counting — yet sits directly within Hunter and Carmody's reassessment (750k to 800k) and the lower-central envelope of Williams's radiocarbon-derived contact estimate (750k to 1,2M) [@anon1984aboriginal; @thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating; @williams2013population]. Crucially, regional densities never violate hunter-gatherer ecological ceilings: even the densest macro-basin, the South-East Coast and Australian Alps, averages 0,418 inhabitants per km² at 1788, well below agrarian thresholds while comfortably accommodating localised clusters exceeding 1 to 2 inhabitants per km² along the Lower Murray, Port Jackson, Gippsland Lakes and Budj Bim wetlands [@bird2019early; @david2024archaeologic].

Cross-checking the benchmark ledger against the continuous spatial raster grids confirms tight post-year-0 convergence: raster totals match HGIS polygon sums to within 0,01% across every slice from year 0 (600.202 raster vs 600.200 benchmark) through 1500 (751.692 vs 751.691) and 1780 (784.052 exact match). Before year 0, the unconstrained prehistoric climatic raster exhibits sharper Mid-Holocene volatility — dipping from 299,3k at 6000BC to 165,7k at 4000BC and 221,1k at 2000BC before converging on 600,2k at year 0 — because global prehistoric interpolation grids under-weight regional Australian Holocene intensification relative to direct archaeological radiocarbon curves [@williams2013population; @crabtree2021landscape]. Anchor totals in Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} therefore supersede raw Early-to-Mid-Holocene raster excursions while preserving raster spatial allocation within each basin.

# Results

## Continental Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 1788)

Australia's Indigenous population grew 3,52-fold across the 11.788 years separating the terminal Pleistocene from European arrival, averaging a long-term compound growth rate of 0,0107% per annum (Figure \ref{fig:australia-trajectory}). Growth unfolded across three measurable phases reflecting post-glacial ecology and technological adaptation. During the Early to Mid-Holocene (10000BC to 5000BC), aggregate population rose by 161,5k (+72,4%) from 223,2k to 384,7k (0,0109% per annum) as warmer, wetter post-glacial climates re-activated interior river systems and coastal groups adapted to rising shorelines. Between 5000BC and year 0, continental numbers climbed by a further 215,5k (+56%) to reach 600,2k (0,0089% per annum), marking the core era of Holocene economic intensification, seed-grinding expansion and estuarine stabilisation [@williams2015holocene; @florin2021pandanus].

Unlike Europe or East Asia, where the Neolithic transition produced abrupt tenfold demographic surges, pre-1788 Australia experienced a durable, continent-wide ceiling governed by broad-spectrum foraging, fire-assisted niche construction and localised aquaculture rather than cereal monoculture. Continental population shares shifted gradually rather than revolutionarily (Table \ref{tab:regional-shares}): the Murray-Darling Basin edged upward from 21,5% of Australia's population in 10000BC to 23,6% in 1788, and the North-East Coast and Cape York grew from 18,8% to 21%, while the Top End declined slightly in relative share from 15,2% to 13,8% and isolated Tasmania fell from 1,4% to 0,8%.

## The Southeastern Riverine and Coastal Core

Across the entire Holocene, Australia's demographic centre of gravity lay in the temperate southeast. The Murray-Darling Basin (1.086.964 km²) was the continent's single most populous basin at every benchmark, expanding 3,85-fold from 48k in 10000BC (0,044 inhabitants per km²) to 82k in 5000BC, 135k at year 0 and 185k in 1788 (0,17 per km², 23,6% of all Australia). Along the braided Murray, Murrumbidgee, Darling and Barwon waterways, permanent billabongs, freshwater mussels, Murray cod, crayfish and abundant waterfowl sustained some of the densest pre-agrarian linear settlements in the world [@thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating]. Deep burial grounds at Kow Swamp (620 inhabitants by 1788) and Roonka on the Lower Murray (510), Pleistocene lunette camps at Lake Mungo (160) and dense flood-plain clusters at Barmah-Millewa (1.120), Gwydir Wetlands (870), Lake Victoria (780) and Menindee Lakes (540) anchor a 14-site archaeological corridor crowned by the stone fish-trap complex of Brewarrina (Baiame's Ngunnhu, 1.450) and the periodic Bunya pine gatherings at Booburrgan Ngmmunge (2.200) on the northeastern watershed rim.

Immediately seaward of the Great Dividing Range, the South-East Coast and Australian Alps (275.121 km²) achieved Australia's highest regional density at 0,418 inhabitants per km² in 1788, expanding 3,59-fold from 32k in 10000BC to 54k in 5000BC, 88k at year 0 and 115k in 1788 (14,6% of the continental total). Warm coastal estuaries, kelp-fringed rocky headlands and volcanic freshwater swamps supported dense, semi-sedentary territorial nations. At Warrane (Sydney Harbour, 1.500), Dyarubbin on the Hawkesbury-Nepean (680), Jervis Bay (790) and Kamay at Botany Bay (390), Eora, Darug and Yuin clans harvested fish and shellfish year-round [@burke2013archaeology]. Farther south, Gunaikurnai communities across the Gippsland Lakes (1.240) maintained ancestral ritual continuity stretching back to the Last Ice Age at Cloggs Cave [@david2024archaeologic], Kulin nations converged on Naarm and Port Phillip Bay (1.150), and Gunditjmara engineers at Budj Bim (920), Caramut (460) and Koroit (410) excavated stone-lined channels and eel ponds supporting clustered stone huts by 4000BC [@williams2015holocene; @salles2024physiography]. Seasonal summer migrations up to the Bogong High Plains (880) linked alpine uplands with coastal and Murray lowlands into a dense regional exchange web.

## Tropical Savanna, Wet Tropics and Monsoonal Northern Australia

Northern Australia supported the continent's second great demographic concentration, driven by summer monsoonal rainfall, fertile mangrove estuaries and diverse marine-terrestrial ecotones. The North-East Coast and Cape York basin (598.813 km²) achieved the fastest proportional growth of any Australian region (3,93x), climbing from 42k in 10000BC to 78k in 5000BC, 122k at year 0 and 165k in 1788 (0,276 inhabitants per km², second highest on the continent and 21% of the total). Two distinct ecological engines powered this total. In the Wet Tropics of the Atherton Tableland (2.150), rainforest Bama nations developed specialised detoxification techniques for toxic cycad and black-bean seeds, maintaining dense village-like camps within upland rainforest clearings [@hocknull2020extinction; @gaete2025megafauna]. Along the subtropical coast, Meanjin and Moreton Bay (1.950) and K'gari (1.650) supported rich estuarine fisheries, while shell-mound complexes at Weipa (1.080), Aurukun (940) and Princess Charlotte Bay (590) lined Cape York's productive coasts. Across the northern maritime frontier, Torres Strait Islanders on Mer (860), Saibai (535), Erub (520), Mabuiag (440), Badu (380), Muralag (350) and Boigu (310) combined dugong and turtle hunting with intensive yam, taro and banana horticulture, bridging Melanesian agriculture and mainland Australian foraging networks.

Westward across the monsoonal littoral, the Gulf of Carpentaria and Top End (909.136 km²) expanded 3,18-fold from 34k in 10000BC to 58k in 5000BC, 86k at year 0 and 108k in 1788 (0,119 per km², 13,8% of the total). Here, human settlement boasted the continent's deepest verified antiquity at Madjedbebe and Nauwalabila [@clarkson2017human; @florin2020first; @florin2021pandanus]. Once Holocene sea-level stabilisation formed vast freshwater paperbark wetlands across the South Alligator and Glyde floodplains after 2000BC, regional populations expanded dramatically around Kakadu (1.920), the Arafura Swamp (1.420), the Tiwi Islands (1.180), the Gove Peninsula (890), Daly River (740) and Groote Eylandt (430). Rock-art complexes in the Wellington Range and Arnhem escarpment record centuries of dense ritual aggregation and, after 1700, recurring maritime trade with Makassan trepangers [@wright2023archaeology].

Further west, the Kimberley and Fitzroy Basin (309.369 km²) rose 2,88-fold from 16k in 10000BC to 26k in 5000BC, 38k at year 0 and 46k in 1788 (0,149 per km²), retaining coastal occupation stretching back 50.000 years [@norman2022human; @shipton2024abrupt] and ancestral networks visible in the human-assisted genetic spread of the Kimberley baobab [@rangan2015genetic], anchored by maritime Bardi-Jawi and Fitzroy riverine communities on the Dampier Peninsula (830). South of the Kimberley, the arid-coastal Pilbara and Western Coast (560.298 km²) increased 2,83-fold from 12k to 34k (0,061 per km²), its population concentrated along intertidal archipelagos and inland river gorges exemplified by the monumental rock-engraving complex at Murujuga (340).

## South-West Australia, the Arid Interior and Insular Tasmania

In the Mediterranean southwest corner of the continent, South-West Australia covering Noongar country (318.147 km²) grew 3,6-fold from 15k in 10000BC to 26k in 5000BC, 42k at year 0 and 54k in 1788 (0,17 per km², matching the Murray-Darling Basin). Deep Pleistocene continuity at Devil's Lair gave way during the Holocene to intensive yam harvesting, estuarine stone fish traps and controlled woodland burning around Boorloo on the Swan River plains (760) and Hutt River yam fields (610), with coastal Menang weir networks extending east to Kinjarling at King George Sound (445) [@gandini2025genomic; @tobler2017aboriginal].

Across the vast dry heart of Australia, low erratic rainfall imposed an absolute ecological brake on density without preventing continuous occupation or continental trade. Together, the Central Arid Western Plateau (1.969.743 km²), the Lake Eyre Endorheic Basin (1.299.106 km²) and the Nullarbor and Southern Gulfs (485.879 km²) covered nearly half the continent (47,6%) yet held just 72k people in 1788 (9,2%). Population rose from 6k to 21k (0,011 per km²) across the Western Plateau, anchored by enduring desert waterholes and rockshelters at Uluru (215), Warburton Ranges (130) and Puritjarra (84). In the Lake Eyre Basin, expansion from 8k to 26k (0,02 per km²) depended on episodic Channel Country floods along Cooper Creek (960) and the Georgina pituri-trading corridor (490), supplemented by central desert oases around Mparntwe in the MacDonnell Ranges (670) and ochre quarries at Ikara in the Flinders Ranges (420). Along the Nullarbor and Southern Gulfs, population grew from 7k to 25k (0,051 per km²), sharply polarised between dense estuarine and coastal populations at Raukkan near the Murray mouth (1.850) and Tarndanya on the Adelaide Plains (820) versus tiny mobile groups relying on Yuldi (Ooldea Soak, 145) and Koonalda flint quarries (105) along the arid Bight [@crabtree2021landscape; @bradshaw2023directionall].

Tasmania and Bass Strait (82.465 km²) stood apart from every mainland trajectory. Cut off when post-glacial seas flooded Bass Strait prior to 10000BC, Tasmanian Aboriginal society experienced neither Pama-Nyungan linguistic diffusion nor the Mid-Holocene arrival of the dingo and small-tool assemblages [@malaspinas2016genomic; @bird2019early]. Borehole temperature reconstructions confirm modest Late Holocene thermal variability across the island [@suman2016late]. Within this cool temperate island ecology, Pleistocene southwest rainforest caves such as Kutikina (58) were abandoned as dense temperate rainforest closed over glacial valleys, while Holocene habitation concentrated along coastal shell-midden belts and fire-maintained eastern savannas at Oyster Bay (750), Nipaluna on the Derwent (640), Kanamaluka in the Tamar midlands (580) and Preminghana in the northwest (530). As a result, Tasmania registered the lowest long-term growth multiple of all eleven basins (1,88x), climbing steadily from 3,2k in 10000BC to 4,2k in 5000BC, 5,2k at year 0 and 6k in 1788 (0,073 per km²).

## Habitation Hierarchy and Colonial Census Reconciliation

Across all 70 catalogued Indigenous habitation complexes, peak estimated aggregation sizes follow a shallow, continuous pre-urban power-law rank-size distribution rather than an urban Zipfian hierarchy (Figure \ref{fig:australia-hierarchy}). Fitting the upper half of the gazetteer (top 35 complexes, spanning 2.200 down to 590 inhabitants) yields a power-law slope $\alpha = 0,43$ ($R^2 = 0,93$), while the full 70-site curve steepens to $\alpha = 0,83$ ($R^2 = 0,72$) as smaller desert rock shelters and Pleistocene refugia taper down to 58 inhabitants at Kutikina. No settlement crossed 2,5k inhabitants, underscoring the absence of centralised urban states alongside the presence of complex multi-clan seasonal capitals and aquaculture hubs.

Placing our 785k contact estimate beside the official historical Indigenous series compiled by L. R. Smith and published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (Table \ref{tab:census-comparison}) illuminates both the scale of post-1788 demographic collapse and the source of early underestimation. Smith's minimum floor of 314,5k in 1788 was derived primarily by projecting backward from nineteenth-century colonial returns — after smallpox, dispossession and frontier violence had already reduced Victoria's Indigenous population to 2.384 by 1861, Tasmania's to 18 officially enumerated survivors on Oyster Cove, and New South Wales's to 16k [@anon1984aboriginal; @thornton1986our; @burke2013archaeology]. Nationally, official counts fell relentlessly from 180,4k in 1861 to 94,6k at Federation in 1901 and hit a trough of 73.828 (73,8k) in 1933 before recovering to 150,1k by 1971. Only in the late-colonised tropics of Queensland (120k in Smith's 1788 table), Western Australia (62k) and the Northern Territory (50k) did colonial-era back-projections approach our eco-hydrological carrying capacities; across Victoria (15k in Smith vs our southeastern and Murray-Darling densities) and New South Wales (48k), early colonial records missed the pre-epidemic majority entirely [@hunter2015estimating; @thornton1986our].

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties qualify pre-1788 Australian demographic reconstructions.

First, no contemporary census was ever taken across Indigenous Australia prior to British colonisation. Every 1788 estimate — whether Smith's 314,5k floor, our 785k regional synthesis or Williams's upper radiocarbon envelope near 1,2M — carries an irreducible uncertainty band of roughly $\pm 20\%$ to $25\%$ [@anon1984aboriginal; @williams2013population; @hunter2015estimating]. Unresolved debates over the exact arrival route and mortality rate of the 1789 Port Jackson epidemic (variola smallpox vs severe varicella chickenpox) mean that southeastern pre-contact densities remain sensitive to epidemiological assumptions [@thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating].

Second, post-glacial sea-level rise between 16000BC and 5000BC drowned roughly one-quarter of Late Pleistocene Sahul, submerging the Arafura Plain, Bassian Plain and broad northwestern shelves [@gomes2015human; @salles2024physiography]. Early coastal habitation records for 10000BC therefore come disproportionately from surviving rocky headlands, offshore islands and inland escarpment shelters such as Madjedbebe, Nauwalabila and Kimberley caves rather than flooded low-stand shorelines [@clarkson2017human; @norman2022human].

Third, radiocarbon summed probability distributions are vulnerable to taphonomic loss and uneven regional excavation [@williams2013population; @curnoe2016deep]. Older open-air riverine camps suffer heavier alluvial erosion than protected sandstone rockshelters, inflating apparent Late Holocene site counts unless corrected for taphonomic decay. Conversely, massive modern archaeological investment in Victoria, New South Wales and coastal Queensland contrasts with sparser survey coverage in the Kimberley (1 catalogued complex in our 70-site register) and the Pilbara (1 complex), requiring basin totals to rely on joint eco-hydrological carrying-capacity modelling rather than raw site counts.

Fourth, the 70 catalogued settlement figures measure peak seasonal or multi-clan aggregation capacity rather than permanent year-round municipal residency. Sites such as Booburrgan Ngmmunge (2.200) and the Bogong High Plains (880) assembled neighbouring nations during rich seasonal harvests before dispersing into smaller foraging bands across surrounding estates, whereas Torres Strait horticultural villages and southwestern Victorian stone-house clusters at Budj Bim sustained much higher residential permanence [@wright2023archaeology; @burke2013archaeology].

# Conclusion

From the close of the Last Ice Age in 10000BC to the arrival of British ships in 1788, Indigenous Australians built a resilient, regionally differentiated continental society across eleven contrasting eco-hydrological basins. Over nearly twelve millennia, aggregate population expanded 3,52-fold from 223,2k (0,028 inhabitants per km²) to 384,7k in 5000BC, 600,2k at year 0 and 785k in 1788 (0,099 inhabitants per km²). Driven by post-glacial environmental recovery, broad-spectrum plant processing, fire-stick landscape management, specialised fisheries and continent-wide kinship exchange networks, this growth took place without continental cereal agriculture yet pushed humid coastal and riverine basins toward high pre-agrarian densities [@florin2020first; @rangan2015genetic; @david2024archaeologic].

Spatial concentration remained the defining structural law of pre-colonial Australian demography. Just four well-watered basins — the Murray-Darling (185k), North-East Coast and Cape York (165k), South-East Coast and Australian Alps (115k) and Gulf of Carpentaria and Top End (108k) — held 73% of Australia's 1788 population on 36,4% of its land, while nearly half the continent across the arid interior sustained just 9,2% (72k) and isolated Tasmania stabilised at 6k. Reconciling archaeological radiocarbon trends, genomic regionalism and epidemiological reassessment of post-1788 virgin-soil epidemics firmly refutes twentieth-century colonial undercounts near 300k, establishing the pre-contact demographic baseline against which the catastrophic nineteenth-century collapse of Indigenous Australia must be measured [@thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating; @tobler2017aboriginal].

# Footnotes

Note 1 (Chronological Convention). Negative benchmark years denote millennia before the Common Era (10000BC and 5000BC), year 0 marks the classical chronological origin, and post-millennial dates use standard calendar years (500 to 1788).

Note 2 (Area Reconciliation). The full coastal-inclusive areal mask spans 7.895.041,9 km² across eleven basins, whereas the strictly terrestrial HydroBASINS Level-6 vector polygon aggregate spans 7.726.164 km²; the 2,1% variance reflects shallow tidal estuaries, offshore cays and coastal raster edge cells.

Note 3 (Historical Series Provenance). Comparative colonial-to-modern figures in Table \ref{tab:census-comparison} reproduce the Australian Bureau of Statistics Historical Population series (HPDC10) based on L. R. Smith (1980), showing why nineteenth-century post-epidemic colonial tallies systematically depressed pre-1788 southeastern baselines relative to archaeological and epidemiological reconstructions.
